why: It gives the ground Yanagawa's canals stand on and the fact that their water is deliberately kept above the tide, which corrects the reading that such channels are tidal. The tide barrier and the non-tidal regime are described in the present tense and undated, and the canal lengths are modern measurements of a modernized system, so what is attested is today's managed regime; the delta and the tidal range are geography and transfer freely.

It states the size the great porcelain kilns reached and that they were shared, which bounds the kiln's length from above. It describes Arita, a specialist porcelain-making district of Edo Japan, not an ordinary town's kiln. It names no kiln site and gives no source for its "100 m or more". The excavated Hizen kilns recorded on public heritage pages (Hasami among them) would carry the figure better; none has been read for this record.

A signed encyclopedia entry by the medieval historian Yokoi Kiyoshi. The siting passage concerns the Sengoku domains, just before the Edo castle towns, rests on a few eastern domains, and is itself hedged ("apparently"); it gives no compass direction and no distance. The riverbed as the leather workers' workplace comes from a different passage, on the medieval "riverbank people" of the Kamakura to Nanbokuchō periods, not the Edo period.
It places Matsue's channel network on its lakeside ground and names it as the castle moat's own spread.

It says where those records were kept and survive: in the houses of the families that served as village officials, nanushi and shoya. Its limits: it speaks mostly of where the papers survive today, not of where they were kept in the Edo period; and it does not keep all of them in the headman's house - the Nipponica entry says the most important official papers were handed from one headman to the next with an inventory, or else kept in wheeled chests (kuruma-nagamochi) in the gōgura, the village's communal storehouse, so they could be saved from fire. It is Japanese only.

It describes a Chinese city on a live river keeping its wharf on the bank and growing its commercial district up from it, which is the arrangement our river capital draws instead of a boat basin. Hankou was one of the empire's great river entrepots, not an ordinary provincial seat, so it shows the extreme of bankside commercial growth.

It describes where such graves stand today: on part of the household's own land, in the middle of a field along the road or in the front garden. It is a present-day tradesman's impression from one trip to one town, not a survey. It dates neither the graves it saw nor the custom. The writer also presents them as a Kanto form, seldom seen in the Kansai, where the village's shared graveyard is the usual form, so it speaks for one region's practice and not all of Japan's; that such graves belonged mostly to long-rooted, influential households is the writer's guess, marked as one on the page.

It is the one page read that says the grass round the graves was cut before Bon, and that in some places it was cut so the spirits could pass - the clearing of a grave's surroundings as a seasonal act. It compiles four other web pages (a temple's page, a travel news site, a trivia site and a Buddhist-altar retailer's page) and does not report any research of its own. Its history is loose: it calls the 8th century the Heian period. So it attests that the practice exists and nothing of its extent or antiquity.

It gives the growth of a Chinese river town's commercial street straight out of its line of wharves, the form our river capital's bankside district copies. Hankou was one of the empire's great river entrepots, not an ordinary provincial seat, and most of the article's body is about the twentieth century; only its Ming paragraph is ours.
It gives the gate-temple at the mouth of Toribeno and the tradition attached to it, the form our funerary complex's entrance follows.

It shows a great temple on a hillside laid out in three terraces, gate and sub-temples below, main halls in the middle, the founder's mausoleum above, with measured sizes of the main hall and gate. A head temple in the old capital is at the top of the range.

A lord's great temple in a provincial castle town, which is nearer the setting's provincial city than any capital temple, and its plan is given building by building. It gives no area for the precinct; and part of the plan it describes is not seventeenth-century fabric: the kitchen-hall (kuri) was rebuilt and the monks' hall returned to its original size in 1985-1996 from excavated foundations, the bath and the privy were dismantled in the Meiji era and are known only from excavation, and the gate is an 1820 rebuild. It is also the memorial temple of the Maeda lords of Kaga, the largest domain in Japan, with 300 koku of temple land, so its plan is the most a provincial great temple could be, not the usual one.

It gives the ground, the number of cloisters and the population of the greatest Buddhist house of a Chinese capital, the upper end of a city temple. The sentence giving the ground, the cloisters and the monks carries no citation in the article, so those figures cannot be traced to a Song record; they are round ones, and the mu it measures in (a Song mu or a modern one) is not said. The market in its courts is firmer: it rests on the two Song texts the article quotes.

A great temple of a prefectural city rather than a capital, laid out building by building with a measured main hall. The ground it gives is the temple's today, the halls are Ming and later rebuildings, and a great port city is still well above the setting's provincial city. Its ground, axis and pagodas rest on the 2004 national register of protected monuments that it cites, and its main-hall figures rest on Fang Yong's 1991 study of that hall.
It attests exposure at both of Kyoto's grounds this page discusses, the first of the three jobs a funerary field did.

It numbers the holders of one hereditary shrine priesthood down to the present holder (84 in the Senge line, 79 in the Kitajima line, both counted through the single line before the two houses split in the 1340s), which is the longest such an office could run, not what a common one did. Its list follows the Senge house's own genealogy, the Izumo kokuso dento ryaku, which the page names as the source of the list. This is the priesthood of a shrine of the first rank, one of the very few houses allowed to keep the ancient title of provincial governor, so it does not show that a village or town shrine's priestly family reached such a count. The count passed eighty only after the Edo period: the page gives the 80th Senge holder's birth as 1845. The numbers count holders, not father-to-son generations: brothers succeeded brothers (the 55th after the 54th, the 81st after the 80th), the page's genealogy marks adoptions, and the page judges six of the early generations to have really been three. The early generations are traditional rather than historical, the first holders being gods, and the page numbers holders inconsistently: it calls the present holder's father both the 83rd and the 84th, Takatoki both the 53rd and the 54th, and Hatayasu both the 23rd and the 24th.

It says in so many words that a priest family's house was walled with a gate, and dates the quarter. It describes the about thirty houses that survive today in a preserved district, so the wall and gate are an old form seen now, and its figure of about 200 houses in the late 17th century is only "said to be". It speaks of one quarter, and that quarter housed the hereditary priest families of one of the great shrines near the capital; a village or small-town shrine's priest household would have been humbler.
It places the gate-temple at the mouth of the funerary ground, the arrangement our funerary complex copies.

It states the half-moon pond's doctrine and its water supply plainly, so the crescent pond's explanation can rest on it instead of on general reading; but closer and fuller sources can be read and were not used - the museum's own Chinese page, of which this is a loose translation (https://thcdc.hakka.gov.tw/1241/12339/1285/2539/post), and Li Xuxian's referenced paper on the half-moon ponds of the Hakka enclosed houses of Meizhou on the mainland (https://www.sinoss.net/upload/resources/file/2024/07/16/35948.pdf). Its limits: it describes the Hakka HOUSE of Taiwan, settled under the Qing, not a mainland village or a whole lineage village; it says itself that no record explains when the ponds began, it gives two reasons for the half shape and hedges both - "most likely" the pond before a school of the examination system, and, "inferred", deference to early rules against surpassing officials; its English is a loose translation (its "metamorphosis fengshui" is apparently the form school of Yang Yunsong), so a phrase quoted from it is the translator's wording, not the museum's; and its account of the water supply is of households standing among fields, which need not hold for a village pond elsewhere.

It describes one waju of the Nobi plain in the Edo period, with a dated count of its culverts and the size of its main drains, which is the only such count read. It names no documents for its counts, and the Nobi waju faced great rivers, so a village polder on a creek would have needed fewer and smaller openings. Its count runs from 1789 into the early Meiji years (1872) and does not say whether its totals stood at one time, and the size it gives for the main drain belongs to a culvert rebuilt several times, in a year it does not give.

It states the problem a sea polder's drainage met - the tide's range, the flats growing until the older land lost its outlet - and where its settlements stood, on the previous stage's sea dike. It dates the serious reclamation to the Edo-period domains, but carries the same work on through Meiji landlords and the state projects of 1933-1978 and 1986. It reads the settlements on the old dikes off today's map of all those stages together, so it does not show that the Edo-period stages alone were settled that way, and it does not date the subsidence it adds to the outlet problem. It does not describe the outlets themselves or say how they were worked.

It says in plain words that the chain pump lifted water out of low fields in flood as well as into them in drought, and ties that to the growth of the Jiangnan polders. It puts the drainage use only broadly, in the Song dynasty in present-day Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Jiangxi and Fujian, and names no period text for it, though it names the Tiangong Kaiwu and Wang Zhen's Nong Shu for other claims. It gives no dated record, named place or count, and does not say where on a polder the pumps stood.

Two signed encyclopedia entries describe the form and give a medieval Japanese notation for the size of a terrace paddy. Kuroda's entry places terrace-building in the setting's own eras, from the late Kamakura period into the early modern. Hoshikawa's entry describes the terrace as it is today (it notes that machines can hardly work it), the old form seen in modern times, and its high walls are those of steep mountain ground, not of every terrace. They give no wall height in meters, and the notation is one example, not a count; the share of paddy land is a modern, undated national figure from the unsigned MyPedia entry.
It carries the gate-temple's own tradition of standing where the living pass to the other world, which is what this page uses the temple for. It does not mention the Odoi rampart.

It describes the method step by step and cites the monograph on the custom, Aono Harumi's 1982 study, the place to take any number or finer detail from. It calls warichi a special custom, found mostly where harvests were unstable - newly reclaimed paddy on the low, wet ground of big rivers' lower courses, and landslide country - while in ordinary villages each farmer's plots stayed fixed, so it models that kind of village and not the usual one. Beyond listing gobanwari ("chessboard division") among the custom's other names, it says nothing about how the redistributed shares looked on the ground - whether they were cut as equal strips or marked - and it describes Japan only.

It gives an official works standing at the fringe of the capital, enlarged to serve the palace building, the case behind our capital's tile works. It gives no distance from the palace. And it describes the imperial capital, whose Ministry-of-Works establishments and gate-signal apparatus a provincial seat had no counterpart of, so the form is stepped down two tiers by us.
